At the back of the house there was a door nobody used.

It opened onto a narrow strip of garden between the kitchen wall and the fence. Nothing much grew there. The sun arrived late and left early; the soil was hard, the stones green with moss. A rusted watering can lay on its side beneath the window, collecting rain. In summer, a small yellow flower appeared between two paving slabs, and each year my mother said, “Well, look at that,” as though the flower had done something personally generous.

The door stuck in its frame. You had to lift the handle and lean your shoulder into it. My father could open it with one hand. He would step outside to take a phone call, or to be alone with a cup of coffee, and the door would close behind him with a soft, satisfied click.

When I was young, I thought the garden was a secret place. I went there to hide from my brother, from chores, from the long afternoons when rain kept us indoors and the clocks seemed to slow down out of spite. I would squat beside the fence and inspect the busy, private lives of ants. I made up stories about the flower, which I imagined had traveled a great distance to arrive beneath our window. It was a brave flower. It had crossed mountains.

Then I grew older and understood that nothing had traveled anywhere. A seed had fallen, the wind had moved on, and the flower had done what flowers do. This seemed less magical until, years later, I understood that ordinary persistence is a kind of magic too.

After my father died, the house became full of small, unanswerable questions. How many teaspoons of sugar had he put in his coffee? Which drawer held the spare batteries? Why had he kept the broken radio, and what was in the box of screws labeled “Important”? Each object seemed to be waiting for him to come back and explain himself.

The back door stuck worse than ever. I stood before it one afternoon, pressing the handle down, lifting it, leaning my weight into the wood. The old motions returned to my body before I knew I remembered them. At last the door gave way.

The garden was smaller than I remembered. The fence had bowed inward. The watering can had rusted through at one corner, and the soil had become a puzzle of roots, gravel, and fallen leaves. But between the same two paving slabs, the yellow flower was there.

I went out without a coat. The air smelled of wet stone. I crouched beside the flower, which had grown crooked toward the window, and saw that its stem was thin but unbroken. I touched nothing. It seemed rude to interrupt.

For a long time I listened to the house behind me. Pipes ticking. The refrigerator humming. A floorboard settling in the hallway. These were not the sounds of a person returning, but they were not nothing. They were the house continuing its work.

My father had liked to say that a thing was only broken if you couldn’t find a use for it. He said it about chairs with loose legs and jars without lids, about radios and old bicycles. He said it about people sometimes, though I don’t think he meant to. I used to believe he was defending clutter. Now I wonder if he was defending the possibility of another life for what had been left behind.

The next spring, I cleaned the garden. I pulled the weeds carefully, leaving the small yellow flower alone. I righted the watering can and set it beneath the window. I didn’t plant anything. I didn’t know what would grow there, and I didn’t want to decide too soon.

On warm days I began to leave the door open. Not wide—just enough to let the kitchen breathe. The cat discovered the garden and treated it as a country newly annexed to his kingdom. The wind carried in the smell of soil. Once, a bee found its way through the gap and blundered around the kitchen window until I lifted the curtain for it.

I am older now than my father was when he died. This fact sometimes arrives quietly, like a guest who has been sitting in the room for hours. I find myself doing the things he did: saving screws, turning off lights, standing outside with coffee when the phone rings. I don’t know whether this is imitation or inheritance. Perhaps the difference matters less than I used to think.

The door still sticks. I could fix it, but I haven’t. There is something reassuring about the small resistance: the need to lift, lean, try again. Some entrances ask for a little effort. Some places are easy to forget until you put your shoulder to the wood.

In the garden, the flower returns each year. It is never in exactly the same shape. Sometimes it grows tall; sometimes it barely clears the stones. I don’t know what mountain it crossed, or whether it crossed one at all. I only know that it is there, making use of the narrow strip of earth it was given.

When I see it, I say, “Well, look at that.”

And for a moment, the whole house seems to listen.
